items.title: Derivation of Expression for Energy Stored in a Stretched Material

source_refs.note: Derivation of Expression for Energy Stored in a Stretched Material: a main subheading of 5.6 Strain energy in deformed materials, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 99-99.

blocks.text: Consider a material in the form of a spring as shown in Fig. 5.6. It is stretched by a force F through extension x. As the extension is directly proportional to the stretching force within the elastic limit, therefore the force increases uniformly from zero to F as shown in Fig. 5.7. Thus, the average force that stretches the spring through Δx is 1/2F. Hence work done by the stretching force will be given as:

blocks.alt: Two springs hang from a horizontal support. The left spring is at its original length (labelled Original length of spring). The right spring carries a slotted-weight load and is longer; arrows between two horizontal lines mark its extension x below the end of the left spring. An arrow F beside the load points down.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.6: A spring of original length stretched by a force F through an extension x (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.6).

blocks.text: Work done = Average force × Distance in the direction of the force
The work done by the stretching force is stored in the spring as its strained energy and is equal to the potential energy stored in its molecules.

blocks.alt: A graph of force F against extension delta x from the origin O. A straight line rises from O to P at force F; a dashed line joins P to the F-axis and a dotted line drops from P to Q on the extension axis. The triangle OPQ is shaded grey.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.7: Force F against extension delta x; the shaded triangle OPQ (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.7).

blocks.latex: \text{Strained energy stored in the body} = E = \frac{1}{2}F.\Delta x = \frac{1}{2}k\Delta x^2
blocks.text_alt: Strained energy stored in the body = E = ½F.Δx = ½kΔx²
